newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: MOTOR RACING-HILL FAILS TO REACH THE STARTING LINE.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HILL FAILS TO REACH THE STARTING LINE.

text.p: Damon Hill gained an immediate introduction to life as a Formula One also-ran when he failed to even reach the starting line at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix on Sunday.
A year after winning in Melbourne at the start of his successful 1996 campaign, the 36-year-old Briton had to watch from the pits as compatriot David Coulthard took the honours at Albert Park.

After barely scraping on to the grid at the rear of the field after a succession of mechanical problems, Hill's worst fears were realised when his Arrows lost power during the warm-up lap because of a fault with the throttle.
"I am philisophical because I always knew it was going to be tough getting reliability," said Hill, who was unceremoniously dropped by Williams mid-way through last season.
"But I thought I would get more than one lap in," he said.
Discarded by the most successful team of recent years, Hill found employment with Arrows, an ambitious team desperate to shed their reputation as perennial losers.
"We knew things were tricky and things were going to go wrong. It was about what we expected," Hill said.

Speaking to reporters in the Arrows pits during the race, a rueful Hill recognised the irony of the situation as German Heinz-Harald Frentzen, the man Williams brought in as his replacement, led the race at the time.
A winner of 21 grand prix titles, including eight last year, in 67 previous starts, Hill said the mechanical failure was not the day's most difficult moment to endure.
"It is not nearly as frustrating as watching the race going on for the lead right now," he said.
Asked his thoughts about watching Frentzen drive a car significantly quicker than the rest of the field, Hill said: "It was me for five years. I know what it is like on the inside.
"I look at the situation (the performance of Williams' cars) dispassionately and try to learn from whatever I am watching."
Rival Mika Hakkinen, who steered his McLaren into third place in Melbourne, had words of sympathy for Hill as a world champion turned back marker.
"I am sure it was not fun for Damon Hill coming from the position he had last year. It is going to be very hard for him this year," the Finn told reporters.
Arrows face an intense period of engine testing before they return for the Brazilian Grand Prix in Interlagos on March 30.
"We have got to go home and start testing and try to get some reliability in the car," Hill said.
"Just about everything needs improving at the moment."
Given Arrows' poor record in terms of reliability and speed, it may be Hill's sense of patience that will need the most attention.
